title: How to view variables while debugging in Xcode on Mac: a complete developer guide
metaTitle: How to view variables while debugging in Xcode on Mac
description: Learn how to view variables while debugging in Xcode on Mac using the built-in debugger, variables view, and LLDB console for efficient software development.
targetKeyword: how to view variables while debugging in xcode on mac
intro: To view variables while debugging in Xcode on Mac, you must use the integrated debugger by setting a breakpoint to pause your application's execution. Once the app is paused, you can inspect the current state of your variables through the Variables View in the debug area or by hovering over code in the editor.
tldr: Set a breakpoint by clicking in the gutter next to your code line.
Run your app in Debug mode to trigger the breakpoint.
Use the Variables View in the bottom panel to inspect values.
Hover over variables in the source editor for quick access.
Use the LLDB console with the 'po' command for deep inspection.

blocks.text: Setting up your Xcode debugging environment

Debugging starts with preparation. Before you can inspect variables, ensure your build scheme is set to Debug. You can check this by clicking the scheme name in the top left toolbar and selecting Edit Scheme. Under the Run action, verify that the Build Configuration is set to Debug. If you are running a Release build, the compiler might remove variables or optimize them away, making them impossible to view.

Breakpoints are the foundation of inspection. Locate the line of code where you suspect an issue. Click the gutter, the narrow column to the left of your line numbers. A blue marker appears. This tells Xcode to halt execution precisely at that spot. You can also press ⌘ \ to toggle a breakpoint on the current line. When the app hits this line, execution stops, and the debug area opens automatically.
Inspecting variables in the debug area

When your app pauses, look at the bottom of the Xcode window. The debug area contains two primary panes. The left pane is the Variables View. It lists all local variables, their types, and their current values. Click the disclosure triangles to expand complex objects like arrays or dictionaries. This view updates in real time as you step through your code.

For faster checks, hover your mouse over any variable name in your source editor. A small pop-up window appears showing the variable's current value. If you need a better look at complex data, select a variable in the Variables View and click the eye icon. This triggers a Quick Look preview, which is helpful for viewing images, colors, or large data structures without cluttering your console.
Advanced inspection with the LLDB console

The right side of the debug area is the console. This is your gateway to LLDB, the low-level debugger. Type po followed by a variable name to print a detailed description of an object. For example, typing po myVariable gives you a human-readable summary of that object. You can also modify values on the fly by typing expression myVariable = 10 to test how your app reacts to different inputs.

Sometimes you might find that variables appear empty or inaccessible. First, check your optimization settings. If the compiler optimization level is set to anything other than None, the compiler might inline variables or delete them entirely to save space. Navigate to your project settings, select your target, go to Build Settings, and search for Optimization Level. Set it to None to ensure all variables remain visible during your debugging session.

If you accidentally close the debug area, you can bring it back with ⇧⌘Y. You can also toggle the inspector pane on the right with ⌥⌘0 to see additional details about the selected object. Keeping your workspace clean helps you focus on the code. Use ⌘0 to hide the navigator and give yourself more room to see the debug output.

items: Force unwrapping optionals that are nil causes a crash before you can inspect them.
Variable scope issues often lead to unresolved identifier errors.
Running Release builds instead of Debug builds hides variable state.
Overly complex breakpoints can significantly slow down your app's performance.
Misspelling variable names in the LLDB console.

blocks.text: Moving forward with your debugging workflow

Debugging is a skill that improves with practice. Once you master viewing variables, start using conditional breakpoints. Right-click an existing breakpoint and select Edit Breakpoint. You can set a condition, like count > 5, so the debugger only stops when that specific situation occurs. This saves time by preventing the app from pausing unnecessarily during loops or frequent operations.

faq.question: Why can I not see my variable values in Xcode?
faq.answer: This usually happens because you are running a Release build. Change your build configuration to Debug in your scheme settings. Also, check that your optimization level is set to None.

faq.question: How do I print a variable in the Xcode console?
faq.answer: Use the LLDB command 'po' followed by the variable name. For example, type 'po myVariable' in the console at the bottom of the screen.

faq.question: What is the shortcut to show the debug area?
faq.answer: Press ⇧⌘Y to toggle the visibility of the debug area in Xcode.

faq.question: Can I change a variable's value while the app is paused?
faq.answer: Yes. Use the 'expression' command in the LLDB console, such as 'expression myVariable = 5', to change the value while the app is paused at a breakpoint.
